summary: Polytechnique Montréal authors partially replicate FeedbackEval (394 Python repair tasks; feedback types test/compiler/simulated-human/simple) with GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, reproducing the original trends within a few points. They then build an exploratory Java extension: 50 CoderEval Java tasks, 100 GPT-4o-mini-injected mutations (50 logical, 50 compile), and JUnit 4 tests translated by GPT-4o-mini. With GPT-4o-mini as the repair model, no feedback type is significantly better for logical bugs; compiler and simple feedback beat simulated human feedback for compile errors; and lighter prompts cost less with no significant accuracy loss.

claims.claim: The FeedbackEval Python findings replicate: average Repair@1 55.55% vs 56.4% (GPT-4o) and 60.2% vs 60.8% (Claude 3.5 Sonnet), with test feedback best.
claims.evidence: Table I matches the abstract numbers. But it is a single run per condition (§VI: 'Each condition was executed once'), and the claim that deviations are 'within expected variability' has no variance estimate behind it. Table II shows simple > test on HumanEval for GPT-4o (79.3 vs 78.7). RQ3 was not replicated.

claims.claim: In Java, test feedback is not superior: simple and JUnit test feedback do not differ significantly for logical mutations.
claims.evidence: Table IV: simple 43/50 (86%), test 41/50 (82%), human 37/50 (74%). Cochran Q(2)=8.00 p=0.0183, but all Holm-adjusted McNemar p>=0.0938 (simple vs test p=0.50). With n=50 the test can't detect small effects; the authors correctly say this is 'insufficient evidence', not equivalence.

claims.claim: For compile-error repair, compiler (javac) and simple feedback significantly outperform simulated human feedback.
claims.evidence: Table IV: compiler 47/50 (94%), simple 46/50 (92%), human 39/50 (78%); Q(2)=12.67 p=0.0018; Holm p=0.0234 and 0.0313. 92% of the compile mutations were syntax errors, so the bugs are easy.

claims.claim: Lighter prompts reduce cost without significant loss of repair effectiveness; CoT costs most.
claims.evidence: Table V: Repair@1 80-88%, Q(6)=5.04 p=0.5392; CoT CAD 0.000575/repair vs baseline 0.000236. Single model (GPT-4o-mini), single run, 50 tasks.

claims.claim: Python conclusions may be sensitive to benchmark construction, feedback representation and tooling (JUnit terseness vs pytest verbosity).
claims.evidence: Offered as a hypothesis only; Java and Python setups differ in mutation source, model and test framework all at once, so the cause can't be isolated. The authors acknowledge this (§VI).

patterns.note: Execution-based test feedback is best in Python but shows no significant advantage over a generic 'code is wrong' prompt in Java with terse JUnit 4 output; compiler feedback is strong for compile errors.
javac diagnostics give 94% repair of compile mutations and significantly beat simulated human feedback (though not simple feedback).
Cost per successful repair reported; lightweight prompts are cheaper with no significant effectiveness loss.
LLM-simulated 'human/expert' feedback is the worst feedback type in both languages.

methodology.sample: Replication: 394 Python tasks (230 CoderEval + 164 HumanEval) x 4 feedback types x 2 models. Extension: 50 CoderEval Java tasks -> 100 mutated instances; 7 prompt variants on the 50 logical instances.
methodology.baselines: The original paper's reported numbers; the 'simple feedback' generic prompt serves as an internal baseline.
methodology.models: Replication: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (the original used 5 models). Extension: GPT-4o-mini only, which also generated the mutations, translated the tests and simulated human feedback. All are dated models for 2026.
methodology.variance: Single run per condition. Wilson 95% CIs, Cochran Q and Holm-corrected exact McNemar tests in the Java extension; no significance tests on the Python replication.
methodology.ablations: Prompt-component ablations (no docstring/context/guidelines/persona) in both parts.
methodology.contamination_controls: None. HumanEval/CoderEval are public and likely in training data; Java mutations come from the same model family that repairs them (acknowledged §VI).

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint (10 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables); no venue stated.
standards.artifacts: GitHub: LouisLalonde/FeedbackEval and leusonmario/LOG6306-EmpiricalStudy (replication package section).

biases.detail: The whole Java extension uses GPT-4o-mini for mutation, test translation, simulated feedback and repair, so the model is effectively grading its own error distribution.
50 Java tasks / 100 instances; with McNemar at n=50 the non-significant results are underpowered.
Each condition run once; replication deviations called 'within expected variability' without measuring it.
Function-level CoderEval/HumanEval repairs; 92% of compile mutations are syntax errors. Nothing repository-level or agentic.
Public benchmarks plus LLM-generated mutations may match the model's training distribution (acknowledged).
Python-vs-Java differences confound language, mutation source, model and test framework, so the 'tooling ecosystem' explanation is a hypothesis.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: OpenAI GPT-4o / GPT-4o-mini and Anthropic Claude 3.5 Sonnet used as subjects; no vendor authors.
coi.funding: NSERC, CIFAR, Canada Research Chairs Program.
coi.detail: Independent academic replication of another group's benchmark.

verdict_reason: An honest, well-reported replication with proper paired statistics and released artifacts, and it is one of few papers that tests Java at all. But the Java part is small (n=50), uses one dated model that also built the benchmark, runs each condition once, and works on function-level tasks. Its main Java result is a non-significant difference, not a demonstrated equivalence.
applicability: Directly relevant as a caution for a Java team building verifier loops. Feeding raw JUnit 4 assertion failures back to the model may add little over a generic 'tests failed' signal. If test feedback is the backbone of the harness's repair loop, make it informative: JUnit 5 or AssertJ messages with expected/actual values, stack traces trimmed to the project's frames, and the failing test source. Measure that on the team's own repositories instead of assuming the Python results carry over. javac/compile feedback is reliably useful, so compile-then-test gating is a safe default and works the same under any agent host. Lighter prompts are cheaper without measurable loss, which supports keeping AGENTS.md/system-spec preambles lean. It says nothing about multi-repo work, spec-driven workflows or agentic (multi-step) repair, and the models are stale.
